opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the first thing that struck me was how small and how hands-on everything felt. Coming from an academic background, I expected research to be split into "idea people" and "implementation people," but at OpenAI there was almost no separation. Everyone wrote code. Very senior researchers would be debugging training runs or digging through infrastructure issues right alongside newer people. There was a strong sense that you couldn't really understand a research problem unless you were close to the actual system.

The second thing was how much the culture valued engineering. In academia, the incentive is often to get a novel idea into a paper, and the code can be a bit of an afterthought. At OpenAI, the bottleneck was usually whether you could make something work reliably at scale. So things like clean infrastructure, fast iteration, and good tooling were treated as first-class research contributions, not just support work. That really resonated with me, because I'd always cared a lot about building good tools.

It was also very goal-driven. Instead of everyone following their own curiosity in a hundred directions, there was a shared sense of "what are the few big bets we're making, and how do we push them forward?" People were pretty willing to drop their own pet projects if something else looked more promising for the main direction.

And finally, there was a lot of trust and ownership. Nobody really told you step by step what to do. You were expected to find the important problems yourself, take responsibility for them, and move fast. That can be a little intimidating at first, but it's also incredibly empowering. You feel like your work actually matters to the final outcome.

r001.rationale: The response describes hands-on, engineering-focused, goal-driven research, but does not say the culture relied more on researchers’ intuition than on systematic methodology.

r002.rationale: It does not mention researchers arriving from Google or attribute a shift toward iterative work to them.

r003.rationale: It mentions fast iteration as a cultural value, but does not state that research success rate increases linearly with iterations per unit time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I first joined OpenAI, the thing that struck me most was how little hierarchy there was in the day-to-day research work. Coming from academia, where there's a fairly clear ladder from student to advisor, I expected something similar. Instead, it felt much flatter. If you had a good idea and could show evidence for it, people listened, regardless of how long you'd been there.

The second thing was the intensity around empirical results. Discussions were very grounded. People would say, "That's an interesting hypothesis, what does the plot look like?" There was a strong bias toward running the experiment quickly rather than debating for weeks. That pushed me to become much more disciplined about building fast, reliable infrastructure, because the bottleneck was usually how quickly you could iterate, not how clever the idea was.

I also noticed a real culture of sharing. Internal docs, dashboards, and training runs were quite open, and people were generous with their time when you asked questions. That openness made onboarding much easier than I expected, even though the scale of the systems was intimidating at first.

And honestly, there was a sense of urgency that I hadn't felt before. People believed the work mattered and that timing mattered, so there was a lot of energy, sometimes to the point of burnout risk. But overall it felt like a place where engineering and research were treated as equally important, and that resonated with me a lot given my background.
